title: Nahum 2:8–13
context: The prophet pictures Nineveh as a pool of water from of old, yet the people flee, and no one looks back though voices cry, “Stop! Stop!” Plunder of silver and gold is taken from a city of endless treasure, and she is left empty, void, and waste. The oracle then asks where the lions’ den has gone, the place where the lion and the lioness walked with the cubs and no one made them afraid; the lion had torn enough for the cubs and filled the dens with prey. The LORD of Armies says he is against her: chariots will be burned, the sword will devour the young lions, prey will be cut off from the earth, and the voice of the messengers will no longer be heard. Versification: English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: But Nineveh has been from of old like a pool of water, yet they flee away. “Stop! Stop!” they cry, but no one looks back.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nineveh has been from of old like a pool of water, yet they flee away. “Stop! Stop!” they cry, but no one looks back. The city, long like a pool, now empties as people flee, and the call to stop cannot hold them. The name Nineveh is spoken again, and the panic is in that failed call.

Arminian readers hear a city that had seemed as settled as a pool, now emptying in flight, a cry that cannot hold the people, a word that still names Nineveh as the one who flees.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the old pool, the flight, the cry to stop, and the refusal to look back as the LORD’s appointed emptying of the city.

Shared ground: Nineveh flees, and no one looks back. The pool image is the verse’s own contrast with the flight.

verses.text: Take the plunder of silver. Take the plunder of gold, for there is no end of treasure, an abundance of every precious thing.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Take the plunder of silver. Take the plunder of gold, for there is no end of treasure, an abundance of every precious thing.” The call is to take silver and gold; the treasure has no end, every precious thing in abundance. The wealth that made the city proud becomes plunder. The taking is named, and the verse does not linger over it.

Arminian readers hear a reversal of endless treasure, a city whose abundance is now an open store for others, a word that answers robbery with loss, still spoken as a public call.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the plunder of silver and gold, and the abundance of every precious thing, as the LORD’s appointed spoiling of the city.

Shared ground: the treasure has no end, and it is taken as plunder. The wealth does not save her.

verses.text: She is empty, void, and waste. The heart melts, the knees knock together, their bodies and faces have grown pale.
verses.arminianNotes:
“She is empty, void, and waste. The heart melts, the knees knock together, their bodies and faces have grown pale.” Three words finish the city’s state: empty, void, and waste. Hearts melt, knees knock, faces grow pale. The fear is told in those bodily signs, and the waste is not described further.

Arminian readers hear a complete emptying, a people whose strength has failed in heart and knee and face, a word that still treats their terror as the fruit of the cruelty the book will later name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the emptiness and waste, and the melting heart, knocking knees, and pale faces, as the LORD’s appointed end of Nineveh’s courage.

Shared ground: she is empty, void, and waste, and fear has taken the people. The line is sober, and it is enough.

verses.text: Where is the den of the lions, and the feeding place of the young lions, where the lion and the lioness walked with the lion’s cubs, and no one made them afraid?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Where is the den of the lions, and the feeding place of the young lions, where the lion and the lioness walked with the lion’s cubs, and no one made them afraid?” The question searches for a den that had seemed safe: lion, lioness, and cubs walking unafraid. Assyria is pictured as a lion’s household, once unchallenged. The figure is a question, not a hunt scene, and it is not enlarged.

Arminian readers hear a taunt that is also a moral question: where now is the den that made others afraid? The safety of the predator is gone, and the question itself is the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the missing den, the feeding place, and the unafraid walking of lion, lioness, and cubs as the LORD’s own question over a power he is bringing down.

Shared ground: the lion’s den is asked for and not found. The next verse will recall how that den was filled.

verses.text: The lion tore in pieces enough for his cubs, and strangled prey for his lionesses, and filled his caves with the kill and his dens with prey.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The lion tore in pieces enough for his cubs, and strangled prey for his lionesses, and filled his caves with the kill and his dens with prey.” The past of the den is a past of tearing and of filled caves, prey enough for cubs and lionesses. The figure names a predatory plenty, and the tearing is told in those clauses without further description.

Arminian readers hear a power that had fed itself on others, a den filled by violence, and a word that still remembers that plenty as guilt, now that the den is being asked for and not found.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the torn prey, the strangled kill, and the filled dens as the LORD’s own account of how the lion-city had lived, the reason the den is now empty.

Shared ground: the dens were filled with prey. The figure stays a lion’s hunt, and it is not turned into a longer scene.

verses.text: “Behold, I am against you,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword will devour your young lions; and I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, I am against you,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword will devour your young lions; and I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard.” The LORD of Armies is against her. Chariots burn, young lions fall by the sword, prey is cut off, and the messengers’ voice ends. The city’s power, its hunt, and its official word all stop.

Arminian readers hear a personal “I am against you” from the LORD of Armies, a closing of the lion figure in fire and sword, and a silence of messengers that still treats the city as one being addressed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the “I am against you,” the burning of chariots, the sword on the young lions, the cutting off of prey, and the ended voice of messengers as the LORD of Armies’ own last word in the chapter.

Shared ground: the LORD of Armies is against her, and the messengers will no longer be heard. The lion figure and the siege end in his saying.
